title: Ammannia baccifera: Spotting Blistering Ammannia in Rice Fields
metaTitle: Ammannia baccifera in Rice: How to Spot and Control It
metaDescription: Ammannia baccifera, or apoy apuyan, grows in irrigated and rainfed rice. Learn to spot its purplish flowers and why common rice herbicides hit it hard.
excerpt: Ammannia baccifera, known in English as blistering ammannia, is a broadleaf weed of irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields in the Philippines. It stands upright with brownish stems and tight clusters of small purplish flowers. This page shows how to spot it in your palay, what harm it can do, and how to control it for good.

blocks.text: What Is Ammannia baccifera?

This weed belongs to the loosestrife family, which holds many plants of wet ground. Farmers in some areas call it apoy apuyan. Ammannia baccifera grows in both irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields, so you can meet it in almost any wet paddy. It comes up between the rice hills and grows upright with the crop.

The plant can live as an annual, finishing in one season, or carry on as a perennial. It also spreads in two ways. First, it makes seeds. Second, pieces of broken stem can take root and grow into new plants. So hand weeding that leaves stem pieces on wet soil can spread the weed instead of killing it. That is why careful weeding matters as much as early weeding.

blocks.caption: Quick facts about Ammannia baccifera
rows: Irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields

blocks.text: How to Identify Ammannia baccifera

Look for an upright, branched plant with brownish stems. Its shape gives it away: the lower branches grow long, and they get shorter toward the top, so the plant looks like a small pyramid. The leaves range from elliptical to lance shaped, pointed at the tip and narrow toward the base. As a broadleaf weed, it has flat leaves with netted veins. Finally, check where the leaves meet the stem for tight clusters of tiny purplish flowers.

items: Upright, branched plants with brownish stems standing between the rice hills.
Long branches near the base and shorter ones near the top, giving a pyramid shape.
Elliptical to lance shaped leaves with pointed tips, narrowing toward the base.
Tight clusters of small purplish flowers along the stem.
Broken stem pieces on wet soil that start to root and grow again.

blocks.text: Why It Hurts Your Palay

This weed competes with your palay for light, water and fertilizer. Because it stands upright and branches, it can shade the lower leaves of young rice and crowd the hills it grows between. The longer it stays, the more food it takes from the crop. Thick patches also give insects, rats and other pests cover close to the rice.

It causes trouble at harvest too. Its seeds can mix with the grain, which lowers the quality of your harvest and carries the weed to new fields. Since some plants persist and broken stems can regrow, a patch you ignore this season may come back stronger in the next.

blocks.title: Its weak spot
blocks.text: Here is good news. This weed gives way easily to herbicides, especially 2,4 D and butachlor. So if you already plan a herbicide spray for other weeds, ask your technician whether a product with one of these fits your field and the age of your rice. Then read the FPA registered label and follow its timing and rate. Spray while the weed is still young for the best result.
How to Control Ammannia baccifera

items: When you hand weed, lift out the whole plant with its roots. Then carry it off the field, because stem pieces left on wet soil can root again.
Do not chop the plant and leave the pieces in the paddy. Cutting only breaks it into fragments that may grow into new plants.
Check the field after each weeding for new shoots coming up from broken stems, and pull them while they are small.
Remove plants before the purplish flower clusters set seed, so fewer seeds build up in the soil.

blocks.text: What to Do at Each Age of Your Rice

items: **0 to 5 days:** keep the soil saturated. Use a pre emergence herbicide only if the field had many weeds last season.
**6 to 10 days:** hand weed in transplanted rice. In direct seeded rice, this is the window for an early post emergence spray.
**11 to 20 days:** keep water in the field, weed by hand or with a rotary weeder, and let Azolla and the Altica beetle help. Spray only if those fail.
**21 to 30 days:** top up the water and keep weeding. Spray only if weeding fails.
**31 to 40 days (transplanted rice):** hand weed. A spray this late is only a rescue.
After any post emergence spray, bring the water back within 1 to 3 days at 3 to 5 cm and hold it for 4 to 5 days. Keep young rice above it.

blocks.text: Active Ingredients That Work on Broadleaves

If water and weeding cannot hold Ammannia baccifera down, choose an active ingredient that works on broadleaves at the age of your rice. The table follows PhilRice recommendations. Shop by the ingredient on the label, never by the brand. If your field also has other kinds of weeds, the [weed control helper](/weeds#control) finds the ingredients that cover all of them.

blocks.title: When a spray stops working
blocks.text: PhilRice notes that this weed is sensitive to herbicide application, particularly to 2,4 D and butachlor.
Spray Safely

Use only herbicides registered with the [Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority](/blog/fertilizer-and-pesticide-authority), and follow the label on the pack: the rate, the timing, the water and the protective clothing. Switch herbicide groups between seasons so the weeds do not learn to survive them. Our [guide to herbicides for rice](/weeds/herbicides-for-rice-weeds) explains the groups.
Keep Ammannia baccifera Out Next Season

items: Plant clean, certified seed. Weed seeds mixed into the punla are the easiest way in.
Keep the seedbed, the canals and the bunds free of weeds, so seed does not wash or blow into the paddy.
Plow and harrow well, and rake out the runners, roots or pieces you turn up. A small piece left in wet soil can grow a new plant.
Pull escapes before they flower and set seed, and carry them out of the paddy instead of leaving them on the bund.
Keep the field clean after harvest and through the fallow, so fewer seeds build up in the soil for next season.

blocks.text: These steps work for every [broadleaf weed](/weeds/types-of-weeds) in the paddy, not only this one. The [weed management guide](/weeds/weed-management-in-rice) puts them in order for a whole season.

blocks.text: Questions Farmers Ask About Ammannia baccifera

items.q: What is Ammannia baccifera called in the Philippines?
items.a: In English it goes by blistering ammannia, and some Filipino farmers call it apoy apuyan. It belongs to the loosestrife family. In the field, you will know it by its upright, pyramid shape, its brownish stems and the small purplish flowers in tight clusters where the leaves meet the stem.

items.q: How do I control it in my rice field?
items.a: Start with clean seed and a level field, so water covers the soil evenly. Hand weed early and remove whole plants, since broken stems can regrow. If you choose a herbicide, pick one made for broadleaf weeds that fits the age of your rice. This weed is sensitive to 2,4 D and butachlor, but always follow the FPA registered label.

items.q: Why does it come back after I weed it?
items.a: It spreads by seed and by stem fragments. When you pull or chop it carelessly, broken pieces of stem stay on the wet soil and grow new roots. Some plants also live on as perennials instead of dying after one season. So remove whole plants, carry them out, and check again a week or two later.
